ov_en: WebLogic XMLDecoder deserialization (CVE-2017-3506/CVE-2017-10271/CVE-2019-2725) allows attackers to send crafted SOAP XML to WLS-WSAT or AsyncResponseService endpoints, exploiting XMLDecoder WorkContext deserialization to execute arbitrary Java code.
vu_en: WebLogic WLS-WSAT and async services use XMLDecoder to parse WorkContext XML in SOAP requests. Because XMLDecoder can instantiate arbitrary Java classes and call their methods, attackers can craft malicious XML to create ProcessBuilder or Runtime instances and execute OS commands.
ex_en: 1. Probe WebLogic version and exposed endpoints (/wls-wsat/, /_async/) 2. Craft SOAP XML with malicious XMLDecoder payload in WorkContext 3. Use ProcessBuilder to execute commands and confirm RCE 4. Write WebShell via PrintWriter for persistent access 5. Execute follow-up operations via WebShell
mi_en: 1. Upgrade to latest patched version 2. Remove or restrict /wls-wsat/ and /_async/ endpoint access 3. Use WAF to filter malicious XML in SOAP requests 4. Restrict WebLogic process privileges 5. Monitor for anomalous SOAP requests and file write operations

ov_en: Brute force is the most fundamental attack method—attempting large numbers of credential combinations to gain account access.
vu_en: Lack of anti-brute-force mechanisms (CAPTCHA, account lockout, rate limiting).
ex_en: Use Hydra or Burp Suite for automated credential testing.
mi_en: Implement account lockout policy and CAPTCHA.

ov_en: Session hijacking exploits web application session management flaws to obtain authenticated user sessions. Common methods include session fixation, session sniffing (HTTP plaintext), session prediction (weak randomness), and XSS-based cookie theft.
vu_en: Common session management flaws: 1) Missing HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite Cookie attributes 2) sessionId not regenerated after login (session fixation) 3) Low-entropy sessionId susceptible to prediction 4) Session cookie transmitted in HTTP plaintext 5) No session timeout or excessively long timeout.
ex_en: 1. Analyze Cookie security attributes 2. Detect session fixation (does sessionId change after login?) 3. Analyze sessionId randomness 4. Attempt network sniffing (HTTP) 5. Combine with XSS for cookie theft
mi_en: 1. Set HttpOnly+Secure+SameSite=Strict on cookies 2. Regenerate sessionId after login 3. Use cryptographically secure PRNG 4. Enforce HTTPS site-wide 5. Set reasonable session timeout 6. Bind session to client fingerprint (IP/UA)

ov_en: Password reset vulnerabilities are among the most common authentication logic flaws, involving predictable reset tokens, token leakage, Host header injection, and parameter tampering—enabling account takeover without knowing the original password.
vu_en: Common password reset flaws: predictable token generation algorithm (e.g., timestamp or user ID based), no token expiration or excessively long lifetime, token not invalidated after use (replayable), reset link URL controlled by Host header (Host Header Injection), short reset code susceptible to brute force, and resetting others' passwords by modifying user identifier parameters.
ex_en: Analyze the complete reset request chain; test token predictability (collect multiple tokens and analyze patterns); attempt Host header injection (set Host to attacker-controlled domain to redirect reset link); test parameter tampering (submit your email alongside target user ID); check if verification code is brute-forceable (4-6 digits, no rate limit).
mi_en: Use cryptographically secure random tokens (at least 128 bits); short expiration (15-30 minutes) with immediate invalidation after use; hardcode reset email domain so it is unaffected by Host header; verification codes at least 6 digits with attempt limits; obtain user identifier from server-side session, not client parameters; log all reset operations with anomaly alerting.

ov_en: OAuth authentication vulnerabilities cover multiple security flaws in the OAuth 2.0 authorization flow: missing state parameter CSRF, authorization code leakage, token hijacking, loose redirect_uri validation, Client Secret leakage, and scope escalation—all potentially leading to account hijacking or unauthorized resource access.
vu_en: Common OAuth 2.0 implementation flaws: loose redirect_uri validation (allowing subpaths or open redirects) leaks auth codes/tokens to attacker endpoints; missing state parameter enables CSRF; auth codes not bound to client allow replay; Implicit Grant exposes access_token in URL fragment; Client ID/Secret hardcoded in frontend or mobile app.
ex_en: Analyze full OAuth flow (capture authorize and token endpoint parameters); test whether redirect_uri can be modified to attacker URL (subpath, URL encoding, open redirect chain); check state parameter presence and server-side validation; search frontend JS and mobile app for leaked Client Secret; test whether Scope can be escalated.
mi_en: Strict exact-match redirect_uri validation (not prefix match); enforce state parameter with server-side validation; use PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) to harden auth code flow; avoid Implicit Grant; never hardcode Client Secret in client-side code; implement token binding and minimum scope policy.

ov_en: SAML authentication vulnerabilities include signature bypass, XML Signature Wrapping (XSW) attacks, assertion injection, and replay attacks. In enterprise SSO environments these allow identity spoofing to log in as any user, potentially affecting the entire enterprise application ecosystem.
vu_en: Common SAML security flaws: lax XML signature verification (validating signature existence without checking what it covers); XSW attacks (relocating the signature to validate a different element than the one actually used); missing Recipient/Audience/NotOnOrAfter attribute validation; replayable assertions; XML comment injection bypassing attribute parsing.
ex_en: Intercept SAMLResponse from normal auth flow (Base64-decode to get XML); analyze signature coverage and assertion structure. Test XSW: copy the legitimately signed element, insert a forged identity in the assertion so signature validation passes but the SP uses the forged one. Test XML comment injection in NameID (admin<!--x]-->@evil.com). Test assertion replay and expiry validation.
mi_en: Use a security-audited SAML library; ensure signature validation covers the actual assertion elements used; strictly validate Audience, Recipient, and NotOnOrAfter attributes; implement assertion ID uniqueness to prevent replay; enforce XML Schema validation on SAML responses; enable encrypted assertions.

ov_en: 2FA bypass techniques target implementation flaws in TOTP, SMS, and email OTP mechanisms—exploiting logic vulnerabilities, brute force, response manipulation, and step skipping. A successful bypass reverts account security to password-only protection.
vu_en: Common 2FA implementation flaws: short code length (4-6 digits) without rate limiting (brute-forceable); 2FA step skippable (direct access to post-auth pages); code not bound to session (can use account A's code to authenticate account B); predictable backup/recovery code generation; client-side response manipulation of success/failure; 2FA state stored in Cookie and deletable.
ex_en: Test step skipping first: after password auth, access post-auth pages without entering 2FA code. Test brute force: analyze code length and failure response (rate limit present?). Test response manipulation: intercept 2FA response and change failure to success. Test session binding: use a valid code from account A to authenticate account B. Analyze backup code format and generation algorithm for predictability.
mi_en: At least 6-digit codes with daily attempt limits (lock after ~5 failures); 2FA state enforced server-side only; codes bound strictly to session and user; backup codes generated with CSPRNG; implement exponential backoff (increasing delay per failure); require 2FA re-verification for critical operations.

ov_en: CAPTCHA bypass techniques target implementation flaws in image CAPTCHAs, sliders, and behavioral verification—exploiting reuse, response leakage, OCR, and logic bypass to re-enable brute force, automated scraping, and bulk registration.
vu_en: Common CAPTCHA implementation flaws: answer returned in HTTP response (hidden field or comment); CAPTCHA verification decoupled from business request (can be sent separately); post-verification token reusable (one pass, multiple uses); simple image CAPTCHA accurately readable by OCR; slider CAPTCHA validation parameters directly constructable.
ex_en: Analyze complete CAPTCHA verification flow. Check if response leaks the answer (view HTML source, HTTP headers, Cookie). Test CAPTCHA reuse (submit the same passed token multiple times). Test whether removing CAPTCHA parameters still passes. Attempt OCR on image CAPTCHAs (Tesseract). Analyze slider request parameters for direct construction.
mi_en: Store CAPTCHA answer server-side only; bind CAPTCHA and business request via a one-time token invalidated after use; use a mature CAPTCHA service (reCAPTCHA/hCaptcha); implement exponential backoff on failures; combine IP reputation, device fingerprint, and behavioral analysis for multi-layer risk control.

ov_en: "Remember Me" persistent login vulnerabilities involve reversible token generation, predictable keys, and deserialization risks in Remember-Me Cookies. Attackers who analyze or forge these tokens achieve persistent identity impersonation. A classic example is Apache Shiro's RememberMe deserialization vulnerability (CVE-2016-4437).
vu_en: Common "Remember Me" flaws: Cookie value uses reversible encoding (Base64) instead of encrypted signatures; default or hardcoded encryption key (e.g., Shiro's default AES key); Cookie contains a Java/PHP serialized object leading to RCE on deserialization; Cookie not bound to client IP or device fingerprint and replayable cross-device; excessively long Cookie lifetime with no forced revocation.
ex_en: Obtain and analyze Remember-Me Cookie (Base64 decode, hex inspect). Check for known framework format (e.g., Shiro) and test default key. Analyze whether Cookie contains a modifiable user identifier (e.g., change user ID or role). Test Java deserialization (replace Cookie with ysoserial payload). Test cross-IP/device Cookie replay.
mi_en: Use cryptographically secure random token as Remember-Me identifier; never store user info in the Cookie; change framework default encryption keys; prohibit Java/PHP serialized objects in Cookies; bind token to client fingerprint (IP+UA+device ID); set reasonable lifetime (max 30 days); provide logout-all-devices function for token revocation.

ov_en: JWT (JSON Web Token) is widely used for authentication in modern web apps and APIs. Its three parts are Header.Payload.Signature. Common attacks include Algorithm None (disabling signature), key brute-force, RS256→HS256 algorithm confusion, and KID parameter injection—all leading to authentication bypass or privilege escalation.
vu_en: Common JWT flaws: 1) Server does not validate alg field (accepts none) 2) Weak secret (brute-forceable) 3) Symmetric/asymmetric algorithm confusion (RS256→HS256) 4) kid field unsanitized (SQL injection/path traversal) 5) exp not validated 6) Sensitive data stored in plaintext payload.
ex_en: 1. Intercept and decode JWT to analyze structure 2. Test Algorithm None attack 3. Attempt HS256 key brute force 4. Obtain public key and test algorithm confusion 5. Test kid parameter injection 6. Tamper with payload privilege fields to verify
mi_en: 1. Strict alg field allowlist 2. Strong random secret (256+ bits) 3. RS256 preferred over HS256 4. Parameterized queries for kid 5. Always validate exp and iat 6. No sensitive data in payload 7. Implement JWT revocation mechanism

ov_en: Arbitrary File Download (Path Traversal) is a common high-severity web vulnerability. When a download function's file path parameter is user-controlled and the server applies no strict filtering, attackers use ../ sequences to read arbitrary server files including configuration files, source code, DB credentials, and SSH keys.
vu_en: The file download endpoint concatenates user-supplied filename/path directly into a filesystem path without canonicalization, whitelist filtering, or sandbox restriction.
ex_en: 1. Identify download endpoint and parameters 2. Test basic path traversal (../) 3. Try encoding bypasses (URL/double/Unicode) 4. Download system sensitive files to confirm vulnerability 5. Target application config files to extract DB credentials 6. Enumerate and download sensitive files in bulk
mi_en: 1. Use file IDs instead of filenames as parameters 2. Whitelist downloadable files 3. Canonicalize path then verify it is within the allowed directory 4. Use chroot or sandbox to restrict file access 5. Strip ../ and all traversal sequences 6. Block downloads from sensitive directories

ov_en: Race condition vulnerability exists in the time window between file upload and security check (deletion). The server typically saves the file to a temporary directory first, then runs security checks; if checks fail the file is deleted. In the millisecond gap between save and delete, high-concurrency access to the malicious file achieves RCE.
vu_en: The server uses a save-then-check flow, and the temporary file is stored in a web-accessible directory, allowing direct URL access before the security check completes.
ex_en: 1. Analyze upload flow and response timing 2. Identify temp file storage path 3. Prepare malicious file (WebShell) 4. Multi-threaded concurrent upload + access 5. Execute malicious code within the race window
mi_en: 1. Store temp files outside web-accessible directory 2. Use random filenames 3. Check-then-save (store in non-web dir, verify, then move) 4. Disable script execution in upload directory 5. Use file locking for atomic operations

ov_en: Path Traversal / Directory Traversal is the most common filesystem vulnerability in web apps. Attackers inject ../ sequences or their encoded variants into file path parameters to break out of the application's intended directory and read (LFI) or even write arbitrary server files. Combined with log injection, LFI can be escalated to RCE.
vu_en: The application concatenates user input directly into filesystem paths without path canonicalization or directory boundary validation.
ex_en: 1. Identify file operation endpoints 2. Test basic ../ traversal 3. Try encoding bypasses 4. Read sensitive system files 5. Attempt LFI→RCE escalation (log poisoning/session inclusion/PHP filter chain)
mi_en: 1. Use file ID mappings instead of direct paths 2. Canonicalize path then verify it is within allowlisted directory 3. chroot to restrict file access 4. Block ../ and all encoded variants 5. Run application with least-privilege

ov_en: Zip Slip is an arbitrary file write vulnerability exploiting path traversal sequences (../) in archive filenames (ZIP/TAR/JAR/WAR). When a server auto-extracts user-uploaded archives without validating filenames, malicious files are extracted outside the intended directory, allowing overwriting of critical configs or writing of WebShells.
vu_en: When decompressing ZIP/TAR files, the server uses the filename recorded in the archive as the extraction path without validating for ../ traversal or checking whether the resulting absolute path stays within the intended directory.
ex_en: 1. Identify ZIP upload and extraction functionality 2. Determine web root or target directory path 3. Craft malicious ZIP with path-traversal filenames 4. Upload to trigger extraction 5. Access written WebShell to confirm RCE
mi_en: 1. Validate each file's target path is within the intended directory before extraction 2. Use Path.normalize() then boundary check 3. Reject filenames containing ../ 4. Extract to sandbox/temp directory and inspect before moving 5. Disable script execution in extraction directory

ov_en: MIME type spoofing is one of the most common file upload bypass techniques. When the server relies solely on the HTTP Content-Type field to determine file type, attackers disguise malicious files (e.g., PHP WebShell) with an allowed Content-Type (e.g., image/jpeg) to pass the type check and store on the server.
vu_en: The server determines file type only via HTTP Content-Type header or magic bytes without deep content inspection (e.g., actually parsing the image) and without restricting script execution in the upload directory.
ex_en: 1. Upload legitimate file and observe behavior 2. Modify Content-Type to test bypass 3. Combine with magic bytes spoofing 4. Exploit web server parsing vulnerabilities (double extension/Nginx parsing) 5. Locate upload path and access WebShell
mi_en: 1. Do not trust Content-Type; use content-based detection (e.g., imagemagick image validation) 2. Whitelist file extensions 3. Rename uploaded files (UUID) 4. Disable script execution in upload directory 5. Separate file storage from web serving

ov_en: Null byte injection exploits C's null-terminated string behavior. When a backend (e.g., PHP < 5.3.4) passes file paths to underlying C functions, injecting %00 truncates subsequent characters, bypassing extension validation and allowing execution of files like .php disguised as .jpg.
vu_en: The backend performs string operations in a high-level language (appending .php suffix, checking extension whitelist) then passes the result to a C-level function to open the file. The C function stops reading at \x00, causing the high-level security check to be bypassed.
ex_en: 1. Check target PHP/Java version 2. Inject %00 in filename 3. Whitelist check sees only the .jpg after %00 4. Actual save/include truncates at %00 to .php 5. Access to verify execution
mi_en: 1. Upgrade to PHP 5.3.4+/latest version 2. Filter \x00 before path operations 3. Use whitelist + UUID rename 4. Never concatenate user input directly into paths 5. Disable script execution in upload directory

ov_en: Web Cache Deception exploits parsing differences between CDN/cache layers and backend servers. When the backend serves /account/x.css as /account (returning user data) but the cache stores the response as static content due to the .css extension, attackers lure victims to that URL and then retrieve the cached sensitive data unauthenticated.
vu_en: Cache layer and backend parse the same URL differently: 1) Backend ignores non-existent path segments 2) Cache determines caching policy by extension 3) Cache policy does not exclude responses containing sensitive data.
ex_en: 1. Probe cache layer and caching policy 2. Find dynamic pages with sensitive information 3. Craft deceptive URL with static file extension 4. Lure victim to URL to trigger caching 5. Retrieve cached data without authentication
mi_en: 1. Set Cache-Control: no-store, private on sensitive pages 2. Cache layer validates Content-Type matches extension 3. Backend returns 404 for non-existent paths 4. Include Cookie/Authorization in cache key 5. CDN configured to only cache explicitly defined static resource paths

ov_en: CDN hides the true origin IP; bypassing the CDN to find the real server IP is an important step in penetration testing.
vu_en: Information leakage via DNS history, subdomains, email headers, or global scanning reveals the origin server IP.
ex_en: DNS history records, subdomain enumeration, email header analysis, global port scanning (e.g., Shodan/Censys).
mi_en: Restrict origin server access to CDN IP ranges only.

ov_en: CL-CL smuggling occurs when front-end and back-end servers handle multiple Content-Length headers differently. RFC 7230 states requests with multiple CL headers should be rejected, but some implementations select one. If the front-end uses the first CL and the back-end uses the second (or vice versa), an attacker can inject a second complete HTTP request inside the first request's body.
vu_en: When receiving a request with multiple Content-Length headers, front-end and back-end select different CL values. One side reads the body using the first CL, the other uses the second, causing part of the data to be treated as the next request.
ex_en: 1. Confirm front-end/back-end architecture 2. Send dual-CL requests to detect discrepancy 3. Craft smuggling payload to inject malicious request into back-end queue 4. Use smuggling to bypass ACL/WAF and access restricted resources 5. Potentially escalate to request hijacking/cache poisoning
mi_en: 1. RFC-compliant: reject requests with multiple Content-Length (return 400) 2. Unify CL parsing logic across front-end and back-end 3. Use end-to-end HTTP/2 4. Front-end normalizes requests before forwarding 5. Disable TCP connection multiplexing (keep-alive)

ov_en: TE-CL smuggling occurs when the front-end proxy prioritizes Transfer-Encoding (chunked) while the back-end prioritizes Content-Length. The front-end forwards the complete chunked data, but the back-end reads only CL bytes, leaving the remainder in the TCP buffer to be treated as the next independent request.
vu_en: Front-end and back-end disagree on TE vs CL priority when both are present. RFC 7230 says TE should override CL, but some back-end implementations prioritize CL.
ex_en: 1. Detect TE vs CL priority discrepancy 2. Craft request with both TE and CL 3. Front-end forwards complete request via TE 4. Back-end truncates at CL; remainder becomes smuggled request 5. Smuggled request bypasses ACL/WAF or hijacks other user requests
mi_en: 1. Unify TE/CL priority across front-end and back-end 2. Reject requests with both TE and CL 3. Use HTTP/2 end-to-end 4. Disable back-end TCP connection reuse 5. Front-end normalizes requests before forwarding
